problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as modeling tail dependence in quantitative risk management and quantifying risk measures such as Value at Risk at high confidence levels. It also focuses on implementing risk-analysis-relevant copulas, especially simple copula families that can capture joint tail behavior for risk aggregation.
problem_statement_quotes: Modern quantitative risk management relies on an adequate modeling of the tail dependence and a possibly accurate quantification of risk measures, like Value at Risk (VaR), at high confidence levels like 1 in 100 or even 1 in 2000.
Our focus here is implementation of simple yet powerful copula models, capable of a satisfactory capturing the joint tail behaviour of the modelled risk factors.

This paper deals with a few simple copula families, including Multivariate B11 (MB11) copula family, presented in (Milek, 2014). We will show that this copula family is suitable for the risk aggregation as it is exceptionally able to reproduce tail dependence structures;
classical_baseline: The paper treats Monte Carlo as the classical baseline for quantifying risk measures, and it also contrasts its copula modeling with the popular Gauss copula. In the risk-modeling context, it presents copula-based risk aggregation as an alternative to modeling the entire multivariate probability density function.
classical_baseline_quotes: Quantum computing makes such a quantification quadratically more efficient than the Monte Carlo method; see (Woerner and Egger, 2018) and, for a broader perspective, (Orús et al., 2018).

Since the 2008 financial crisis the financial market regulators require a satisfactory modeling of the tail dependence, which should be superior to the one of the popular but criticized Gauss copula, see (MacKenzie and Spears, 2014), which asymptotically vanishes, unless the correlation approaches one.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the Monte Carlo method is less efficient for quantifying risk measures, and that the Gauss copula is criticized because its tail dependence asymptotically vanishes unless correlation approaches one. It also notes that as the copula dimension grows, the number of canonical copulas increases quickly, creating combinatorial complexity and under-determined parameterization issues.

This complexity is the source of MB11 copula flexibility, as each of its multivariate tail dependence coefficients can be adjusted, to some degree, separately, see (Milek, 2014). The number of the copula coefficients will, for n>3, exceed the number of the tail dependence coefficients. This will lead to an under-determined problem, however, a unique copula parameterization can still be found, e.g., by using convex optimization within Maximum Entropy method of (Jaynes, 2003), see (Dai Pra et al., 2013) for a very similar setup (but in a different context, namely of Bell inequalities for quantum states).
business_stakes: The paper says the motivation matters for risk-based economic capital and for financial institutions being protected against adverse yet probable losses. It also notes that regulators require satisfactory tail-dependence modeling in internal models.
business_stakes_quotes: In this area models of various risk types are aggregated to quantify risk-based economic capital, necessary for financial institutions to be protected against adverse yet probable losses.
